scenes.title: Execution Plans
scenes.narration: An execution plan is the roadmap the database engine follows to run your query, and learning to read it is the single most valuable performance skill.

scenes.title: What a plan tells you
bullets: The physical operators the optimizer chose to satisfy your query
The estimated number of rows flowing between each step
The relative cost of each operation so you can spot the expensive ones
scenes.narration: A plan reveals which physical operators the optimizer picked to satisfy the query. It shows the estimated row counts flowing between steps, which tells you where the data volume explodes. And it assigns a relative cost to each operation so you can quickly spot the expensive parts.

scenes.title: Ask for the plan
scenes.code:
EXPLAIN
SELECT o.order_id, o.total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.region = 'EU'
  AND o.order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01';
scenes.narration: Prefixing any query with EXPLAIN returns the plan without running the statement. Here we join orders to customers and filter by region and date. The optimizer will report how it intends to access each table and how it will combine them.

scenes.title: How to read a plan
steps: Read the tree bottom-up and inside-out
Find the leaf operators that access tables first
Follow rows upward through joins, sorts, and aggregates
The topmost node returns the final result
scenes.narration: A plan is a tree, and you read it from the bottom up and from the inside out. The leaf operators that touch the tables execute first. Rows then flow upward through joins, sorts, and aggregates until the topmost node produces the final result.

scenes.title: Access and join operators

left.title: Access methods
points: Sequential / table scan reads every row
Index scan walks the index in order
Index seek jumps straight to matching keys

right.title: Join methods
points: Nested loop is good for small inputs
Hash join suits large unsorted sets
Merge join needs both inputs sorted

scenes.narration: Access operators range from a full sequential scan that reads every row, to an index scan, to an efficient index seek that jumps directly to matching keys. Join operators trade off in a similar way: nested loops win for small inputs, hash joins handle large unsorted sets, and merge joins are cheap when both sides are already sorted.

scenes.title: Red flags to hunt for
bullets: A full scan on a large table where a seek was expected
Expensive sort or hash operations spilling to disk
Estimated rows wildly different from reality (bad cardinality)
scenes.narration: Watch for a full scan on a large table when you expected an index seek, which usually means a missing or unused index. Be wary of costly sorts or hashes that spill to disk. And distrust plans where the estimated row counts are wildly off, because bad cardinality estimates lead the optimizer to pick the wrong strategy.

scenes.text: Read plans bottom-up, watch estimated rows and costs, and treat a big-table full scan or a misestimated join as your first tuning target.
scenes.narration: Read plans from the bottom up, keep an eye on estimated rows and costs, and treat a large full scan or a badly estimated join as the first thing to tune.
